artboards.title: The same relationship on a phone
F — What each supplier is for

annotations.text:
PRODUCTS × SUPPLIERS — SIX WAYS TO DRAW IT

The relationship is a bipartite graph with weighted, dated, sparse edges: 6 products, 4 suppliers, 24 possible quotes, 12 of them actually known. Every direction below is that same graph, projected differently — and each projection answers one question well and hides another.

A  MATRIX — who quotes what, and who is cheapest. The blanks are the finding.
B  LINKAGE MAP — the shape of the buying. Centrality, specialists, single threads.
C  SPREAD LADDER — where choosing wrong actually costs money.
D  DEPENDENCY — what breaks if one supplier stops answering.
E  FRESHNESS — how old the answer is. The check on all the others.
F  SMALL MULTIPLES — what each supplier is FOR, one card each.

A is drawn at full console fidelity because it is the one that earns the page. B–F are direction sketches: enough to judge, not built.

THE ONE HARD PALETTE CALL

The house rule says the accent appears ONCE per screen — it is the one thing to do next. But a matrix wants to mark six cheapest cells, and six oxide marks would make the accent mean nothing.

So cheapest is NOT the accent. It is a 2px verdigris edge plus a heavier figure — "good", which is what cheapest genuinely is. The single oxide element in the page body stays the action: ask for the 12 prices you have never asked for. (The logo tile and the active rail item are chrome, and are oxide on every screen in the app.)

Same reasoning on the phone: the accent is the one button that does something, not the cheapest row.

820px is a SWITCH, not a reflow.

A matrix does not survive 390px — and neither does a node-link map. The phone answers the same question one product at a time: suppliers stacked cheapest first, actions visible at 44px, and the supplier who was never asked named rather than dropped.

IF ONLY ONE SHIPS

A + E together. The matrix is the screen; freshness is a toggle on it, not a page of its own — on a healthy price book that grid is nearly blank and earns no space.

D is the one worth building next: it is the only direction that answers a question the shop cannot answer today at all, and it needs no new data.

B is the most striking and the least durable — it is legible at 4×6 and a hairball at 40×400. Ship it filtered to one category, or as one supplier's own threads, or not at all.

EVERY FIGURE HERE IS DERIVED, NOT INVENTED.

All six artboards read the demo book in seedData() in index.html — the 4 suppliers, 6 products and 12 price rows, and their real dates. Nothing was made up to make a chart look better, which is why half the matrix is empty and the whole book is 60–66 days old. Those are findings about the seed data, not decoration.

On real shop data the shapes change: the matrix goes sparser, the linkage map gets denser, and the freshness grid is the one that stops being all red.
